The method `org.apache.commons.math3.complex.Complex.reciprocal` returns `NaN` when the input complex number is `NaN`, has both real and imaginary parts equal to `0`, or when the input complex number is infinite. In the case of an infinite input complex number, the method correctly returns `Complex.ZERO`.

Given the bug report mentioning that `Complex.ZERO.reciprocal()` returns `NaN` but should return `INF`, it indicates that there might be an issue in the definition of `Complex.ZERO`.

The definition of `Complex.ZERO` initializes a new `Complex` object with real and imaginary parts set to `0.0`.

Based on the bug report, the test `Complex.ZERO.reciprocal()` should return `Complex.INF`, but it currently returns `NaN`. This discrepancy suggests that the issue might be related to how the reciprocal operation is handled for a `Complex` object with zero real and imaginary parts.

Next, I will inspect the code snippet for the `Complex` constructor to see if there are any special cases or checks that might affect the reciprocal calculation for the zero complex number.

The `Complex` constructor sets the `isNaN` flag if either the real or imaginary part is `NaN`, and sets the `isInfinite` flag if either the real or imaginary part is infinite.

In this context, when `Complex.ZERO` is created with real and imaginary parts both set to `0.0`, the `isNaN` flag will not be set, but the `isInfinite` flag will also not be set because neither real nor imaginary parts are infinite.

This suggests that the reciprocal calculation for `Complex.ZERO` may be incorrectly handling the case when both the real and imaginary parts are `0.0`, leading to the unexpected result of `NaN` instead of `INF`.

To determine the root cause of the issue, I will review the reciprocal calculation logic in the `Complex` class to identify why it's returning `NaN` instead of `INF` for `Complex.ZERO`.
